messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 36
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Detective
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
- Pcl5: 74

**Patient Vignette: Mr. A.**

Mr. A., a 36-year-old South Asian man, sits at the edge of the chair in my office, his posture rigid. He is a detective with the city’s major crimes unit, a job he describes with a hollow pride. He comes to therapy at his wife’s insistence. She has threatened to leave, he says, not because of an affair or addiction, but because of what happens to him at night.

The story begins not in a precinct interrogation room, but in the kitchen of his childhood home in a suburban enclave. He is the eldest son of a respected engineer and a homemaker. To the outside world, his family was a model of immigrant success. Inside, his father’s discipline was a precise, predictable machine. Mr. A. recalls the smell of cardamom tea and the sound of his mother’s bangles clicking nervously. The trigger was always a perceived failure: a B-plus on a math test, a forgotten chore, a tone of voice deemed disrespectful. The punishment was a leather belt, applied to his back and thighs. He learned to stand perfectly still, to not cry, to dissociate into the pattern on the linoleum floor. His mother would look away. He never told a teacher. He learned that silence was survival.

Now, at 36, silence has become a cage. At work, he is known as a “closer.” He can sit in a room with a hardened suspect for sixteen hours, his face a mask of calm detachment. He reads people’s tells—a twitch, a shift in posture—with preternatural accuracy. He believes this skill came from reading his father’s mood in the tilt of his head. But the cost is immense. When a case involves a child, even as a witness, his stomach seizes. He feels a cold sweat prickle his scalp. He recently had to excuse himself from an interview with a twelve-year-old boy who had been beaten by his stepfather. In the bathroom, Mr. A. stared at his own reflection, his hands trembling, seeing not his own face but the face of a terrified child.

The hypervigilance is constant. He cannot sit with his back to a door in a restaurant. He catalogues every exit in a room within seconds. His sleep is a battlefield. Three or four times a week, he wakes up drenched in sweat, his heart hammering, having just heard the *snap* of the leather belt against his own skin, or worse, against the skin of his own two children. He does not hit them. He would rather cut off his own hand. But the fear that he might, that the monster is genetic, lives in his bones.

He avoids his parents. He sends his wife to handle phone calls. When his mother recently visited, he felt a rage so pure and hot it scared him. He did not speak to her for three days. He avoids physical intimacy with his wife. When she touches his back, he flinches. He has not told her the full truth of his childhood. He has told her “it was strict,” a euphemism that feels like a lie.

His negative beliefs are absolute. “I am fundamentally broken,” he says. “I am a fraud. If people knew what I came from, they would see I have no right to judge anyone.” He feels detached, even from his own successes. He solved a triple homicide last year. He felt nothing. He drinks two glasses of whiskey most nights to quiet the noise in his head, to make the flashbacks stop. He is irritable with his children, snapping at them for small noises, then retreating to the garage, flooded with shame.

The PCL-5 score of 74 is not a number to him. It is the weight of a lifetime of holding still, of being a good boy, of building a career out of the ashes of his own terror. He is here, he tells me, because he is tired of being a detective in his own life, always looking for evidence of his own guilt. He is tired of the silence.
